cases.holding: Because R.C. 2151.421 commands designated professionals to report and R.C. 2151.99 criminally penalizes the failure to do so, the statute 'expressly imposes liability' within R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) and 2744.03(A)(6)(c), stripping a political subdivision and its employees of statutory immunity for a failure to report.
cases.quote: we hold that within the meaning of R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) and 2744.03(A)(6)(c), R.C. 2151.421 expressly imposes liability for failure to perform the duty to report known or suspected child abuse

relevance.INP-01: This is the Ohio Supreme Court's controlling statement that R.C. 2151.421 creates an enforceable duty on mandated reporters, with civil consequences for the employing subdivision when it is breached.
relevance.INP-02: The decision turns on the mandatory-reporter list in R.C. 2151.421(A); it marks the boundary between the compelled report and the merely permitted third-party report under R.C. 2151.421(B).
relevance.INP-06: It fixes the legal weight of a report received through the statutory intake channel by making non-reporting actionable against the subdivision.
relevance.INP-07: Physicians and other health professionals are among the R.C. 2151.421(A) reporters whose failure to report the case can expose their public employer to liability.
relevance.INP-08: School personnel were the non-reporters in Campbell, making it the anchor case for the education-disclosure trigger.
relevance.DEC-01: Because non-reporting is actionable, screening decisions that rest on a report that was never made carry statutory consequences upstream of intake.
relevance.FAIL-04: When a child is seriously harmed after a professional failed to report, Campbell supplies the immunity exception that permits a damages claim against the subdivision.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the principal Ohio authority permitting civil recovery where a failure to report preceded a child's death or serious injury.

cases.case_name: Yates v. Mansfield Bd. of Edn.
cases.holding: A board of education may be held liable under former R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) when its failure to report a teacher's sexual abuse of one student in violation of R.C. 2151.421 proximately results in the same teacher's sexual abuse of a different student.
cases.quote: R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) requires designated persons to "immediately report" their "knowledge or suspicion" that a child "has suffered or faces a threat of suffering" any injury indicative of abuse or neglect

relevance.INP-01: Yates states the reporting trigger itself — immediate report on knowledge or suspicion, including threatened as well as completed harm — which is the operative standard at this node.
relevance.INP-02: It explains that persons outside the R.C. 2151.421(A) list are permitted but not required to report, defining the voluntary-report category by contrast.
relevance.INP-07: The Court grounds the duty in the reporter's special relationship with children, the same rationale that governs treating clinicians.
relevance.INP-08: The reporters here were school employees, and the Court extended the protected class beyond the single identified child to other students exposed to the same abuser.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the leading Ohio case allowing recovery where a suppressed report allowed a known abuser continued access to children.
relevance.OUT-06: Yates supplies the proximate-cause framework when later serious harm is traced to an unmade mandatory report.
relevance.PMC-04: The opinion articulates the preventive purpose of mandatory reporting that fatality and near-fatality reviews are meant to enforce.

cases.holding: In a suit over a child's death, the Court held that a public children services agency and its employees owe no R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) duty to cross-report an incoming referral to law enforcement, that R.C. 2919.22 does not expressly impose liability on them, and that employee immunity is lost only for recklessness, which requires a perverse disregard of a known risk rather than mere negligence.
cases.quote: a public children services agency and its employees, upon receipt of a case referral, do not have a duty under R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) to cross-report the case to a law-enforcement agency

relevance.INP-01: O'Toole limits the reporting statute's reach as applied to the agency itself, which is the entity receiving rather than making the report.
relevance.INP-02: It clarifies that the agency's obligations on receiving any report, including a citizen report, are governed by its own statutes rather than by the reporter's duty.
relevance.INP-03: This is the controlling Ohio holding that the receiving agency has no statutory duty to refer the case on to police.
relevance.INP-06: It governs what the agency must do once a hotline or referral comes in, and what it is immune from failing to do.
relevance.INP-10: The recklessness standard defines when escalation or non-escalation of an intake exposes the caseworker to liability.
relevance.DEC-01: A decision to screen out or not escalate is shielded unless the caseworker perversely disregarded a known risk.
relevance.DEC-02: The opinion sets the liability floor for how an accepted referral is investigated by agency staff.
relevance.ACT-06: The case arose from a failure to act on medical indicators of injury, framing the agency's exposure when urgent care is not arranged.
relevance.FAIL-04: This is the leading Ohio Supreme Court decision on agency and caseworker immunity when a child dies under agency supervision.
relevance.OUT-06: It states the standard a family must meet — recklessness, not negligence — to reach the merits after a child fatality.
relevance.PMC-04: The case illustrates why fatality review rather than tort litigation is the practical accountability route in Ohio.

cases.holding: County children services board investigation records kept under R.C. 5153.17 and 2151.141 are 'official records' subject to the sealing provisions of R.C. 2953.52, and the prosecutor who failed to object timely could not relitigate the sealing order later.
cases.quote: records of a county children services board investigation made pursuant to R.C. 5153.17 and 2151.141 are "official records" within the ambit of the sealing provisions of R.C. 2953.52

relevance.FAIL-06: It establishes that CPS investigative files are subject to judicial sealing, which is the mechanism by which an exonerated person can force records out of circulation.
relevance.PMC-04: It defines the statutory character of the investigation file that fatality and systemic reviewers must work from.
relevance.PMC-05: Any transparency analysis of Ohio CPS records must start from this classification of R.C. 5153.17 files and the sealing regime attached to it.

cases.case_name: Kyser v. Summit Cty. Children Servs.
cases.holding: A children-services agency's disposition substantiating a child-abuse allegation is not a final order appealable under R.C. 2506.01, because recording the substantiation in SACWIS does not by itself determine the subject's rights, duties, privileges, benefits or legal relationships, so the common pleas court lacked jurisdiction over the appeal.
cases.quote: a public children-services agency's disposition on a child-abuse allegation under R.C. 2151.421 is not appealable under R.C. 2506.01

relevance.INP-09: It shows that the SACWIS record created at disposition is treated as an internal data entry rather than an adjudicated determination for review purposes.
relevance.INP-10: The decision defines the legal status of the outcome of an escalated screening once the agency finishes its assessment.
relevance.DEC-01: An unsubstantiated or screened-out result is likewise not an appealable administrative order under this reasoning.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling Ohio authority that a substantiated finding carries no R.C. Chapter 2506 administrative appeal — the single most important fact for a family at this node.
relevance.FAIL-06: It limits the individual's ability to force correction of an agency record through the courts.
relevance.PMC-02: It shows the substantiation data feeding state and federal reporting is not tested by administrative appeal.
relevance.PMC-05: The opinion describes what SACWIS entries legally are, which frames what can be demanded or corrected.
relevance.PMC-06: Any cross-analysis of Ohio substantiation data must account for the absence of an appellate check on those entries.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Clough v. Franklin Cty. Children Servs.
cases.holding: The Court denied a parent's mandamus petition for her children-services file because the records are confidential by statute and she made no showing of good cause outweighing the confidentiality interest, and she could not seek records she had never requested before filing.
cases.quote: The good cause shown must outweigh the considerations underlying the confidentiality requirement.

relevance.INP-06: It protects the confidentiality of the intake and referral material, including reporter information, absent a good-cause showing.
relevance.DEC-03: A parent contesting a substantiated finding cannot obtain the underlying file without satisfying this good-cause balancing test.
relevance.FAIL-06: This is the operative Ohio Supreme Court test governing when non-disclosure of a CPS file becomes unlawful.
relevance.PMC-03: It marks the statutory limits on outside review of individual case files by non-party reviewers.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the leading Ohio decision on public-records and mandamus access to children-services records.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Cincinnati Enquirer v. Jones-Kelley
cases.holding: The Court granted mandamus compelling the Department of Job and Family Services to release a requested database, holding the custodian failed to carry its burden of showing the records fell squarely within a statutory exception and that a later amendment excluding foster-caregiver information did not apply retroactively.
cases.quote: A custodian does not meet this burden if it has not proven that the requested records fall squarely within the exception.

relevance.INP-09: It is the decision that pried open the state child-welfare database for outside scrutiny, the classic oversight trigger.
relevance.FAIL-06: It places the burden of justifying non-disclosure squarely on the agency, so silence or generalized confidentiality claims are a transparency failure.
relevance.PMC-01: Performance monitoring depends on the state-level data this case made accessible.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and misuse-of-funds analysis depends on obtaining agency datasets under this standard.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen reviewers rely on the same public-records burden allocation to obtain agency material.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the leading Ohio authority on public-records access to child-welfare agency data.
relevance.PMC-06: Automated cross-analysis of Ohio child-welfare data rests on the disclosure obligation this case enforces.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Cincinnati Enquirer v. Bloom
cases.holding: Interpreting the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision independently, the Court held that it creates a presumption of public access to juvenile delinquency proceedings which a statute cannot override, so a juvenile proceeding may not be closed without an individualized determination balancing the competing interests.
cases.quote: the open courts provision provides a presumption of public access to juvenile delinquency proceedings

relevance.INP-09: It is the constitutional basis for outside observation of juvenile court practice in Ohio.
relevance.FAIL-06: Blanket statutory closure or sealing, applied without individualized findings, is now a constitutional transparency failure.
relevance.PMC-02: Public access to proceedings is a precondition for meaningful external audit of juvenile court practice.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review of juvenile justice and child-welfare practice depends on the access presumption recognized here.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the most recent and most significant Ohio transparency ruling on juvenile court proceedings.
relevance.PMC-06: Any systemic analysis of Ohio juvenile court outcomes depends on the access presumption this case establishes.

cases.holding: Except for narrowly defined statutory exceptions the state must have made reasonable efforts to reunify the family before parental rights are terminated, but the specific R.C. 2151.419(A)(1) reasonable-efforts determination applies only at the enumerated removal and disposition hearings and not at a hearing on an R.C. 2151.413 permanent-custody motion, where the agency must prove reasonable efforts only if it has not already done so.
cases.quote: we hold that, except for a few narrowly defined exceptions, the state must have made reasonable efforts to reunify the family prior to the termination of parental rights

relevance.INP-12: R.C. 2151.419 requires the court to make a reasonable-efforts finding at the hearing that follows emergency protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: The opinion ties the emergency-removal decision to the agency's burden of proving efforts to prevent removal under R.C. 2151.419.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary services offered before court involvement are the principal way an agency satisfies the reasonable-efforts obligation described here.
relevance.ACT-02: The case plan and court-ordered services are the statutory vehicle for the reasonable efforts the Court requires.
relevance.ACT-03: Removal to foster care must be preceded and accompanied by proven efforts to prevent or end the out-of-home placement.
relevance.ACT-05: Less intrusive protective dispositions are part of the reasonable-efforts continuum the Court describes across R.C. 2151.412, .414(E)(1) and .419.
relevance.FAIL-03: Reasonable efforts is the federal Title IV-E and ASFA condition on funding, and this case states how Ohio implements it.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification is the outcome the reasonable-efforts requirement exists to pursue.
relevance.PMC-01: Reasonable-efforts findings are a CFSR measurement point, and this case defines when Ohio courts must make them.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed permanent custody to the agency where the father's untreated pedophilia posed an ongoing risk under R.C. 2151.414(E)(2) and the mother was unable to protect the children under R.C. 2151.414(E)(14), holding the best-interest determination was supported by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: The state has the right to intervene when the exercise of her rights presents a safety or health hazard to her children.

relevance.DEC-03: K.H. shows what evidence of ongoing, untreated parental risk will support a finding that a child cannot safely remain, even where a parent has not personally abused the child.
relevance.ACT-02: It measures a non-offending parent's compliance with a relapse-prevention and protection plan as part of the court-ordered services analysis.

cases.holding: The Court reversed a termination of parental rights that rested solely on the parents' cognitive disability, holding that a child's best interest may not be determined solely on the basis of the parents' limited cognitive abilities.
cases.quote: We hold that the termination of appellants' parental rights based solely on mental retardation does not comply with R.C. 2151.414.

relevance.ACT-06: The psychological evaluations that drove the outcome below illustrate the limits on using clinical assessment as a proxy for parental unfitness.
relevance.FAIL-05: This is the controlling Ohio authority that disability alone cannot justify removal or termination, the core disability-discrimination protection in the chain.
relevance.OUT-02: It constrains the R.C. 2151.414 best-interest analysis by forbidding termination grounded solely on a parent's cognitive limitations.

cases.holding: A juvenile court may not find that a child cannot or should not be placed with either parent unless it finds by clear and convincing evidence that at least one of the then eight enumerated R.C. 2151.414(E) factors exists; general concerns outside the list will not do.
cases.quote: permanent custody may not be granted unless the trial court finds clear and convincing evidence that one or more of the eight enumerated factors in R.C. 2151.414(E) exist

relevance.ACT-02: It ties the case plan to the statutory factors, because failure to remedy the conditions causing removal must be proved under R.C. 2151.414(E)(1).
relevance.OUT-01: Where no enumerated factor is proved, the statute presumes the child can be returned within a reasonable time.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the foundational Ohio holding that permanent custody requires a specific, enumerated statutory finding proved by clear and convincing evidence.

cases.holding: R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) requires a juvenile court to consider each listed best-interest factor but not to discuss each one expressly, so long as the reviewing court can discern from the decision and judgment entry that the factors were considered.
cases.quote: we hold that R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) does not require a juvenile court to expressly discuss each of the best-interest factors in R.C. 2151.414(D)(1)(a) through (e). Consideration is all the statute requires.

relevance.FAIL-01: It sets the threshold a parent must meet to get a permanent-custody judgment reversed for inadequate findings, and it is the current standard of appellate review.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the governing Ohio statement of how the R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) best-interest analysis must be documented at termination.

cases.holding: The agency need not prove that no suitable relative was available before permanent custody may be granted; the availability of a placement that would avoid termination is one relevant factor in the R.C. 2151.414(D) weighing, not a controlling one.
cases.quote: The statute does not make the availability of a placement that would not require a termination of parental rights an all-controlling factor.

relevance.ACT-03: It confirms that a foster placement may become the permanent plan without the agency having to disprove every less restrictive alternative.
relevance.ACT-04: This is the controlling Ohio holding on how much weight a proposed kinship placement carries against permanent custody.
relevance.OUT-03: Families urging guardianship or relative custody instead of termination must understand that Schaefer denies that option automatic priority.

cases.holding: Due process does not entitle a parent whose rights have been terminated to file a delayed appeal; Ohio's existing procedures, including the expedited appeal timelines, are constitutionally adequate.
cases.quote: We therefore hold that Ohio's current procedures comport with due process and that a delayed appeal is not constitutionally required to protect the parent's interest.

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the decisive Ohio authority on appellate timeliness after termination: a missed appeal deadline is ordinarily fatal, which makes the 30-day window the single most important date for a parent.

cases.holding: An order that denies the agency's motion for permanent custody, terminates the agency's temporary custody and awards legal custody to a parent is a final, appealable order under R.C. 2505.02 because it affects the substantial rights of the parties and ends the proceeding.
cases.quote: In contrast, a parent does have a substantial right in the custody of his or her child.

relevance.ACT-02: It frames court-ordered services against Ohio's ASFA timetable, under which a parent has roughly twelve months to remedy the conditions that caused removal.
relevance.ACT-03: It explains why continued temporary foster placement, unlike a final custody award, does not end the proceeding.
relevance.FAIL-01: It defines which agency-adverse and parent-adverse custody rulings can be appealed at all.
relevance.FAIL-03: The opinion describes Ohio's codification of ASFA's 12-of-22-month permanency rule, the federal compliance standard at this node.
relevance.OUT-01: An award of legal custody back to a parent is the reunification disposition the Court treats as final and appealable.
relevance.OUT-04: The Court's concern with children languishing in care is the policy driver behind extended-care and permanency planning.
relevance.PMC-01: The 12-of-22 permanency clock discussed here is a core CFSR permanency measure.

cases.holding: Once an agency with temporary custody moves for permanent custody, a juvenile court has no authority to order a planned permanent living arrangement that the agency has not requested, because that disposition leaves the child in limbo and delays a permanent home.
cases.quote: Children who age out of foster care lack the emotional support system and the financial stability of a permanent custody or adoptive relationship.

relevance.ACT-03: It limits the dispositions a court may impose over the agency's objection once a child is in foster care under temporary custody.
relevance.FAIL-03: The Court's reliance on AFCARS data and federal permanency policy makes it the Ohio expression of the federal anti-drift requirement.
relevance.OUT-04: This is the leading Ohio Supreme Court statement of the harms of aging out and of the disfavored status of the planned permanent living arrangement.

cases.holding: An order continuing temporary custody is not a final, appealable order, because although a juvenile custody hearing is a special proceeding the order must also affect a substantial right, and the continuation of temporary custody does not foreclose appropriate relief later.
cases.quote: While a juvenile custody hearing is a special proceeding, a juvenile court order must also affect a substantial right to be a final, appealable order under R.C. 2505.02(B)(2).

relevance.FAIL-01: It tells a family which interim juvenile court rulings can be challenged immediately and which must wait, the gateway question for any appeal.
relevance.OUT-05: It distinguishes an order that ends the case from one that merely continues it, which controls when a dismissal or closure becomes reviewable.

cases.holding: An adjudication that a child is abused, neglected or dependent implicitly determines the unsuitability of both custodial and noncustodial parents, so no separate parental-unsuitability finding is required before a juvenile court awards legal custody to a nonparent, though the adjudication does not permanently foreclose a later change of custody.
cases.quote: abuse, neglect, or dependency adjudications implicitly involve a determination of the unsuitability of the child's parents

relevance.DEC-05: Filing an abuse, neglect or dependency complaint is what unlocks nonparent custody without a separate unsuitability hearing, which is the practical consequence of the petition decision.
relevance.ACT-04: It is the controlling authority permitting a kinship or nonrelative legal custody award after adjudication without a further unsuitability finding.
relevance.OUT-03: Legal custody or kinship permanency in a dependency case rests on this holding rather than on the Perales/Hockstok private-custody framework.

cases.holding: In a private custody dispute a trial court must make an on-the-record parental unsuitability determination before awarding legal custody of a child to a nonparent, and that determination is made once, at the time of the legal custody hearing.
cases.quote: A parent should be given only one unsuitability determination, which should come at the time of the legal custody hearing.

relevance.ACT-04: When kin seek custody outside an abuse, neglect or dependency case, Hockstok requires an express unsuitability finding first.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the controlling Ohio standard for transferring custody to a nonparent caregiver as a permanency outcome outside the dependency track.

cases.holding: An adjudication of dependency followed by an award of temporary custody to a children services board is a final, appealable order, and the Court grounded that conclusion in the fundamental liberty interest and paramount right of suitable parents in the custody of their children.
cases.quote: Parents have a "fundamental liberty-interest" in the care, custody, and management of the child.

relevance.INP-04: When a court's own referral leads to a dependency adjudication and temporary custody, Murray makes that order immediately reviewable.
relevance.INP-12: It supplies the Ohio Supreme Court's statement of the constitutional interest that emergency protective custody intrudes upon.
relevance.DEC-04: Any emergency removal must be measured against the fundamental liberty interest Murray identifies.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective and temporary custody dispositions short of termination still burden the parental interest Murray recognizes and are appealable.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the state-law counterpart to the federal substantive due process interest invoked in wrongful-removal claims.

cases.holding: Adjudicatory and dispositional hearings must be held separately in a dependency case in which parental rights may be terminated, the Rules of Evidence apply strictly at adjudication, and dependency must be proved there by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: The issue at the adjudicatory stage of a dependency case is whether petitioner has proven, by clear and convincing evidence, that the child is in fact dependent.

relevance.INP-04: A court-generated referral still has to be tested in a separate, evidence-bound adjudicatory hearing before any disposition follows.
relevance.DEC-03: It fixes the burden and the evidentiary rigor that a substantiated allegation must survive once it reaches court.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the foundational Ohio case on the bifurcated adjudication/disposition structure that a filed petition sets in motion.

cases.holding: The statutory sunset date does not automatically divest a juvenile court of jurisdiction, but where the problems that gave rise to the original complaint have been resolved or sufficiently mitigated the court may not enter further dispositional orders on that complaint.
cases.quote: Where the original problems have been resolved or sufficiently mitigated, courts may not make further dispositional orders based on the original complaint.

relevance.OUT-01: Once the conditions that caused removal are corrected, the court loses the basis for continued orders and the case must move toward return home.
relevance.OUT-04: It limits how long an agency can keep a child under orders derived from a stale complaint.
relevance.OUT-05: This is the leading Ohio authority requiring closure when the original basis for the case no longer exists.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Allen Cty. Children Servs. Bd. v. Mercer Cty. Common Pleas Court, Probate Div.
cases.holding: A probate court may exercise its exclusive original jurisdiction over an adoption petition even while a juvenile court is exercising continuing jurisdiction over the same child, because the juvenile court's continuing jurisdiction does not divest the probate court of adoption jurisdiction.
cases.quote: The juvenile court must hold an adjudicatory hearing—generally within 30 days after the complaint was filed—to determine whether the child is abused, neglected, or dependent.

relevance.INP-04: The opinion lays out the statutory sequence and deadlines a juvenile court must follow once a complaint or referral reaches it.
relevance.INP-11: It is the Ohio Supreme Court's framework for allocating jurisdiction between courts with competing claims over the same child.
relevance.DEC-05: It states the 30-day adjudicatory deadline and hearing sequence that filing a petition triggers.
relevance.OUT-03: Where kin pursue adoption or guardianship in probate court while a dependency case is open, this case governs which court may act.

cases.holding: Denial of an indigent parent's request for appointed counsel in a probate adoption proceeding is a final, appealable order, and equal protection is violated by giving indigent parents appointed counsel when their rights are terminated in juvenile court but not when they are terminated by adoption in probate court.
cases.quote: the child and the child's parents are statutorily entitled to legal representation, including a right to appointed counsel if they are indigent, at all stages of the proceedings

relevance.DEC-05: It states Ohio's statutory right to counsel at every stage of a juvenile abuse, neglect or dependency case, which attaches as soon as the petition is filed.
relevance.OUT-02: It extends appointed counsel to indigent parents contesting a stepparent or private adoption that would terminate their rights.

cases.holding: De minimis monetary gifts from a biological parent to a child are not maintenance and support under R.C. 3107.07(A), and the petitioner bears the burden of proving the failure to support and its lack of justifiable cause by clear and convincing evidence, with a dual standard of appellate review.
cases.quote: A probate court determination of whether a financial contribution constitutes maintenance and support for purposes of R.C. 3107.07(A) is reviewed for an abuse of discretion

relevance.OUT-02: Where adoption proceeds without parental consent, this case sets the burden of proof and the standard of review that decide whether the parent's veto survives.

cases.holding: A child victim's statements made for purposes of medical diagnosis or treatment are admissible under Evid.R. 803(4) regardless of whether the child has been found competent to testify, and their admission did not violate the Confrontation Clause.
cases.quote: the child's statements may be admitted at trial as an exception to the hearsay rule pursuant to Evid.R. 803(4) if they were made for purposes of medical diagnosis or treatment

relevance.INP-07: It defines the evidentiary weight that a child's disclosure during a medical encounter will later carry, which is why the healthcare setting matters so much at intake.
relevance.DEC-02: How an investigative interview is framed — treatment-directed or forensic — determines whether the child's statements are later admissible.
relevance.ACT-06: Statements made in the course of emergency medical or psychological evaluation receive this hearsay exception.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, Tenth Appellate District
cases.holding: The juvenile court erred as a matter of law by transferring jurisdiction over an Indian child to the tribal court despite a parent's objection and without addressing 25 U.S.C. 1911(b) good cause, and it must hold an evidentiary hearing on whether good cause exists to deviate from the 25 U.S.C. 1915(b) placement preferences and on the child's best interests.
cases.quote: The juvenile court erred as a matter of law in disregarding the parental veto, disregarding the good cause provision of 25 U.S.C. 1911(b), and transferring jurisdiction to GRIC's tribal court.

relevance.INP-11: This is the leading published Ohio appellate decision on ICWA notice, tribal intervention, the parental veto over transfer, and good cause under 25 U.S.C. 1911(b).
relevance.ACT-04: It requires an evidentiary finding of good cause before an Ohio court departs from ICWA's extended-family and tribal placement preferences.
relevance.FAIL-05: Failure to apply ICWA's notice, transfer and placement provisions is the principal form of unlawful differential treatment of Native families in the Ohio chain.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, First Appellate District
cases.holding: Affirming in part and reversing in part custody dispositions for four siblings, the court held that where reunification within a reasonable time was not possible the mandatory disposition of R.C. 2151.414(D)(2) applied, and it explained that sufficiency review asks whether the evidence justified the juvenile court's findings under the clear-and-convincing standard.
cases.quote: Our sufficiency review asks whether enough evidence exists to justify the juvenile court's relevant findings under a clear-and-convincing standard.

relevance.ACT-02: It reviews whether the parent's performance under the case plan supported the court's findings about reunification within a reasonable time.
relevance.ACT-05: It addresses the range of dispositional alternatives, including protective supervision and remand of custody, available short of permanent custody.
relevance.FAIL-01: It states the sufficiency and manifest-weight standards an Ohio appellate court applies when a parent challenges a custody or permanent-custody judgment.
relevance.OUT-05: It shows when an appellate court will set aside a disposition and return custody rather than let the case close on the agency's terms.

cases.case_name: Kovacic v. Cuyahoga Cty. Dept. of Children & Family Servs.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: Ohio social workers who entered a home and removed children without a warrant were not entitled to qualified immunity on the children's Fourth Amendment claims because a warrantless removal requires exigency, not merely probable cause, although the workers retained absolute immunity for preparing the temporary emergency care order and initiating the proceedings.
cases.quote: The relevant question is whether there was exigency, not probable cause: in the absence of exigency, a warrant is required, even "when probable cause is clearly present."

relevance.INP-03: It addresses the joint police and caseworker entry that typically accompanies a law-enforcement referral in Ohio.
relevance.INP-12: It is the controlling Sixth Circuit case, arising in Cuyahoga County, on the constitutional limits of emergency protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It states the exigency test an Ohio agency must satisfy to remove a child before obtaining a court order.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the leading Ohio-origin Section 1983 decision on warrantless removal of children, and the starting point for any wrongful-removal claim in this circuit.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit held that social workers are bound by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement when entering a home and that no social-worker exception exists, but granted qualified immunity because that rule was not clearly established in the circuit at the time of the entry.
cases.quote: we agree that a social worker, like other state officers, is governed by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement

relevance.INP-03: It governs the common situation where a caseworker accompanies officers to a home following a law-enforcement referral.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a screening into a home investigation triggers the warrant requirement unless consent or exigency exists.
relevance.INP-12: It is the circuit's foundational statement that emergency entry by a caseworker is constrained by the Fourth Amendment.
relevance.DEC-02: Once a report is accepted for investigation, entry into the home requires consent, exigency or a warrant, and the agency bears the burden on consent.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the rule that makes warrantless entries and removals by caseworkers actionable, subject to qualified immunity.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview of a child during a child-abuse investigation, requiring at a minimum reasonable suspicion of abuse, and the court affirmed denial of qualified immunity on the children's Fourth Amendment claims and on the parents' Fourteenth Amendment claims arising from a coercive in-home safety plan.
cases.quote: a social worker must have a reasonable suspicion of child abuse before conducting an in-school interview when no other exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement applies

relevance.INP-05: It shows that a parent's apparent cooperation with a caseworker's plan is not voluntary consent when it is obtained under threat of removal.
relevance.INP-08: It is the controlling circuit authority on interviewing children at school without a warrant or parental consent.
relevance.DEC-02: It sets the minimum evidentiary predicate for the investigative interview of a child once a report is accepted.
relevance.DEC-06: A non-court 'alternative response' built on a safety plan can itself violate due process if it is coerced.
relevance.ACT-01: This is the leading circuit case on the constitutional limits of so-called voluntary in-home safety plans.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: Because the father had consented to the initial removal and safety arrangement, no clearly established law put the caseworker on notice that her conduct violated the family's Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment rights, and qualified immunity was granted.
cases.quote: Absent certain exigent circumstances, the state's termination of or interference with parental rights—even temporarily—requires some measure of procedural protection, like proper notice and an opportunity for a hearing.

relevance.INP-05: It shows how a parent's request for help or agreement to a plan is later treated as consent that forfeits procedural protections.
relevance.DEC-04: It states the notice-and-hearing rule that applies whenever removal is not justified by exigency.
relevance.DEC-06: It is the most recent circuit guidance on consent-based, non-court interventions and the risk that consent defeats later constitutional claims.
relevance.ACT-01: Families entering voluntary services should understand that documented consent is what most often ends a later damages claim.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the boundary of the wrongful-removal claim: consent, not exigency, decided the case.

cases.case_name: Brent v. Wayne Cty. Dept. of Human Servs.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: Social workers who initiate child-removal proceedings are absolutely immune for their role in preparing and presenting the removal petition, even from allegations that they knowingly made false statements, though immunity does not extend to the manner of executing a removal order.
cases.quote: The doctrine of absolute immunity applies even if social workers make knowingly false statements in the petition for a removal order and while advocating before the court.

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling circuit rule that defeats most damages claims premised on falsehoods in the removal petition, and it tells families to attack the execution of the removal rather than its initiation.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Before a State may sever the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that it support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence; a fair preponderance standard is unconstitutional in a permanent neglect proceeding.
cases.quote: Evaluation of the three Eldridge factors compels the conclusion that use of a "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard in such proceedings is inconsistent with due process.

relevance.DEC-03: It is the federal constitutional floor that makes clear and convincing evidence, not a preponderance, the standard once the state moves to sever the relationship.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling federal authority behind Ohio's clear-and-convincing requirement in R.C. 2151.414.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Dept. of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause does not require appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding; the need for counsel is assessed case by case against the presumption that a right to appointed counsel arises only where physical liberty is at stake.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.DEC-05: It is the federal floor for the right to counsel when a petition is filed, a floor Ohio exceeds by statute in R.C. 2151.352.
relevance.FAIL-01: Because the federal right to counsel is conditional, Ohio claims of ineffective assistance in these cases rest on the state statutory right rather than on Lassiter.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: An unwed father was denied due process and equal protection when his children were taken from him under a presumption of unfitness without any hearing on his fitness as a parent.
cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.INP-12: It is the foundational federal authority that a hearing must precede or promptly follow the state's taking of a child.
relevance.DEC-04: It forbids removal based on a categorical presumption about a parent rather than an individualized determination.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: As applied, a statute authorizing any person to petition for visitation over a fit parent's objection violated the mother's due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody and control of her children.
cases.quote: the application of § 26.10.160(3) to Granville and her family violated her due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of her daughters

relevance.INP-05: A fit parent's own request for or refusal of services is entitled to the presumption of correctness Troxel describes.
relevance.DEC-06: Non-court interventions must respect the fit parent's presumptive authority over the child's care.
relevance.ACT-01: It is the constitutional backdrop for treating voluntary services as genuinely voluntary rather than as a condition imposed on a fit parent.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: ICWA's heightened termination standard in 25 U.S.C. 1912(f) does not apply where the parent never had custody of the Indian child, and 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where terminating the parent's rights would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family.
cases.quote: we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling federal construction of ICWA's active-efforts and heightened-termination provisions that an Ohio court must apply once a child is identified as an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-05: It marks the outer limit of ICWA's protections, and therefore where claims of unequal treatment of Native families will and will not succeed.

cases.holding: In a juvenile court custody action between a parent and a nonparent under R.C. 2151.23(A)(2), a parent may be denied custody only on a finding, supported by a preponderance of the evidence, of abandonment, contractual relinquishment of custody, total inability to provide care or support, or other unsuitability meaning that an award of custody would be detrimental to the child; the judgment was reversed because the trial court made no unsuitability finding.
cases.quote: a preponderance of the evidence indicates abandonment, contractual relinquishment of custody, total inability to provide care or support, or that the parent is otherwise unsuitable

relevance.ACT-04: This is the source decision for the unsuitability requirement that Hockstok restates, and it enumerates the only four grounds on which kin or another nonparent may displace a parent outside a dependency case.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency with a nonparent caregiver in the private-custody track rests on this preponderance-of-the-evidence unsuitability finding rather than on a free-standing best-interest comparison.

cases.holding: After a child has been adjudicated dependent, a juvenile court need not make a separate finding of parental unfitness before awarding permanent custody under R.C. 2151.353(D); such an award is justified only when it is in the child's best interests, because a parent's fitness is one factor and parental interests are subordinated to the child's welfare.
cases.quote: we conclude that an award of permanent custody, pursuant to R. C. 2151.353(D), is only justified when it is in the "best interests" of the child

relevance.DEC-03: Cunningham is the source of the proposition In re K.H. echoes — that parental rights are not absolute and yield where the child's welfare requires — and it holds that no separate unfitness finding is needed once a child has been adjudicated dependent.
relevance.ACT-03: The Court treats permanent commitment as the most serious dispositional alternative and reads R.C. 2151.01(C) to permit separating a child from parents only when necessary for the child's welfare or public safety.

cases.holding: Former R.C. 2151.413(A) required a children services agency to have had current temporary custody of the child for at least six months immediately preceding the filing of a motion for permanent custody, and because the agency had not, the trial court had no authority to grant permanent custody.
cases.quote: we believe that given the seriousness of permanently divesting a parent of the right to raise a child, the procedural requirements of former R.C. 2151.413(A) should be strictly construed

relevance.ACT-02: Hayes fixes the minimum length of the parent's opportunity to remedy the conditions that caused removal before the agency may move for permanent custody, and it is the case that supplies the 'every procedural and substantive protection the law allows' framing later borrowed in C.W. and H.F.
relevance.OUT-01: The waiting period exists to give parents a final chance at reunification, and the Court held that an agency may not bypass it by relying on an earlier, non-continuous period of custody.

cases.holding: Under R.C. 2151.352 as clarified by Juv.R. 4(A) and 2(Y), a child who is the subject of a proceeding to terminate parental rights is a party to that proceeding and is therefore entitled to independent counsel in certain circumstances, so the juvenile court erred in refusing to consider full independent representation for a child whose expressed wishes conflicted with the guardian ad litem's recommendation.
cases.quote: child who is the subject of a juvenile court proceeding to terminate parental rights is a party to that proceeding and, therefore, is entitled to independent counsel in certain circumstances

relevance.DEC-05: Once a petition is filed the child is a party in his own right, so the right-to-counsel analysis at this node is incomplete unless it covers the child's entitlement to counsel independent of the guardian ad litem.

cases.holding: An adjudication of abuse, dependency or neglect coupled with an award of temporary custody under R.C. 2151.353(A)(2) is a final order that must be appealed within 30 days under App.R. 4(A), and App.R. 4(B)(5) gives no second opportunity to appeal that adjudication after the final dispositional order terminating parental rights.
cases.quote: App.R. 4(B)(5) does not apply to adjudication orders that include a finding of neglect, abuse, or dependency and a grant of temporary custody to a children services agency

relevance.FAIL-01: H.F. is the third pillar of the Adams/C.B./B.C. line: the adjudication order is final when entered, so a parent who waits for the permanent-custody judgment forfeits every challenge to the adjudication.
relevance.OUT-05: It distinguishes the orders that end the controversy when entered from those that leave issues pending, which controls when an adjudication or closure becomes reviewable.
relevance.ACT-03: A parent contesting the placement of a child in agency temporary custody must appeal the adjudication-and-temporary-custody entry itself rather than wait for a later disposition.

cases.holding: An agency may move for permanent custody on the R.C. 2151.414(B)(1)(d) '12 of 22' ground only if the child had already been in agency temporary custody for twelve of a consecutive twenty-two-month period when the motion was filed; time between filing and the hearing does not count, and a juvenile court lacks authority to grant the motion on that ground otherwise.
cases.quote: an agency must afford parents the full 12-month period to work toward reunification before moving for permanent custody on R.C. 2151.414(B)(1)(d) grounds

relevance.ACT-02: C.W. is the Ohio Supreme Court's construction of the twelve-of-twenty-two-month ground, and it fixes the full twelve months as the parent's guaranteed time to work the case plan.
relevance.OUT-01: It protects the reunification window by refusing to let the months between the filing of the motion and the hearing count toward the statutory period.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is Ohio's authoritative construction of the ASFA permanency clock codified in R.C. 2151.414(B)(1)(d), the federal compliance benchmark at this node, and the brief should rest on it rather than on dicta in In re C.B.
relevance.OUT-04: It defines how long a child's temporary out-of-home placement must run before the permanency ground ripens, and forbids an agency from accelerating that clock.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Renfro v. Cuyahoga Cty. Dept. of Human Servs.
cases.holding: The Court denied mandamus to foster parents seeking a children services agency's child-abuse investigation report, holding that R.C. 2151.421 makes such reports confidential and removes them from R.C. 149.43, that they are exempt from R.C. 1347.08 as investigatory material compiled for law-enforcement purposes, and that the R.C. 5153.17 confidentiality duty — while not absolute — barred inspection absent an overriding right such as a parent's fair-trial interest.
cases.quote: keeping foster care records confidential, not disclosing them, is respondent's primary responsibility under the statute

relevance.INP-06: Renfro is the earlier Ohio Supreme Court holding that a report of suspected abuse and the investigation file it generates are confidential and outside the public-records law.
relevance.DEC-03: A person contesting an agency finding reaches the file only through a recognized override, such as the fair-trial interest recognized in Davis where the agency relies on those records to obtain custody.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the foundation of the confidentiality line that Clough later builds on, and it states the agency's baseline duty as nondisclosure rather than release.
relevance.PMC-05: Any Ohio transparency analysis of children-services records starts here, with the three statutes — R.C. 149.43, 1347.08 and 5153.17 — that Renfro holds do not compel release.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Scripps Howard Broadcasting Co. v. Cuyahoga Cty. Court of Common Pleas, Juv. Div.
cases.holding: The Court granted mandamus compelling a juvenile judge to release the transcript of a contempt proceeding held in his juvenile case, holding that the right of public access extends to transcripts as well as live proceedings and that Juv.R. 37(B) could not be applied to withhold the transcript without the findings required by In re T.R. that access could harm the child and that the harm outweighs the benefits of access.
cases.quote: The right of access includes both the live proceedings and the transcripts which document those proceedings.

relevance.INP-09: Outside scrutiny of juvenile court practice depends on access not only to hearings but to the transcripts that document them, which is what this case secured.
relevance.PMC-02: Meaningful audit of juvenile court practice requires the underlying record, and this decision establishes that access to an open proceeding carries access to its transcript.
relevance.PMC-03: The press obtained the transcript only because the required closure findings were never made, which is the same failure a citizen reviewer can invoke.
relevance.PMC-05: This is Ohio's pre-Bloom framework for public access to juvenile proceedings and their records, and it is the baseline against which Bloom's constitutional presumption must be measured.

cases.case_name: State ex rel. Plain Dealer Publishing Co. v. Geauga Cty. Court of Common Pleas, Juv. Div.
cases.holding: The Court granted prohibition against a juvenile judge's closure order, holding that although there is no qualified constitutional right of access to juvenile delinquency proceedings and such proceedings are neither presumptively open nor presumptively closed, the person seeking closure bears the burden of proving the T.R./Lias factors, and closing proceedings on unsupported findings is an abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: the person seeking closure of a juvenile delinquency proceeding bears the burden of proving the existence of the factors specified in T.R. and Lias

relevance.INP-09: It states the pre-Bloom rule that juvenile proceedings are neither presumptively open nor presumptively closed, the baseline for outside observation of Ohio juvenile courts.
relevance.PMC-03: The allocation of the burden to the party seeking closure is what allows a citizen or press reviewer to resist a blanket closure.
relevance.PMC-06: Systemic analysis of Ohio juvenile court outcomes depends on this burden allocation, which prevents courts from closing categories of cases without evidence.
relevance.FAIL-06: Closing a juvenile proceeding on findings unsupported by evidence, or on a judge's personal predilections, is an abuse of discretion correctable by prohibition — a transparency failure with a remedy.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for an Ohio caseworker, holding that where parents voluntarily consent to a safety plan placing their children outside the home and never use the plan's stated mechanism to revoke that consent, no pre-removal hearing is required and there is no procedural due process violation.
cases.quote: the Smiths needed to explicitly withdraw the consent they explicitly gave, thus requiring Children's Services to either return the children or file a formal complaint against them

relevance.INP-05: It is the counterweight to Schulkers: a parent's agreement to a plan is treated as continuing consent until the parent affirmatively revokes it, and displeasure or repeated questions do not amount to revocation.
relevance.DEC-06: This is the controlling Ohio-origin circuit authority that a genuinely voluntary, non-court safety plan defeats a procedural due process claim, and it is the case Bambach relies on for the rule.
relevance.ACT-01: Families entering voluntary in-home services need to know the operative mechanics: consent must be revoked explicitly, which forces the agency either to return the child or to file a formal complaint.

cases.case_name: Pittman v. Cuyahoga Cty. Dept. of Children & Family Servs.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of immunity to an Ohio caseworker, holding her absolutely immune for the juvenile complaint and the affidavits she filed in her advocacy capacity, and qualifiedly immune on the father's substantive and procedural due process claims because Ohio law places responsibility for placement decisions and for notice of custody proceedings on the juvenile court rather than on the caseworker.
cases.quote: it is the juvenile court's responsibility to ensure that Pittman received adequate notice of the custody proceedings

relevance.ACT-03: Placement decisions belong to the juvenile court, and Ohio law gives a parent the means to contest placement at the dispositional hearing and to propose a change to the case plan at any time.
relevance.ACT-04: A parent or relative whose caregiver-approval process is halted has no damages claim against the caseworker for that decision, because the placement determination is the court's to make — the source decision Brent applies.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc in an Ohio case, the court reversed summary judgment based on absolute immunity, holding that a caseworker is absolutely immune only for acts performed as a legal advocate and not for out-of-court administrative or investigative conduct, so a caseworker who allegedly concealed from the juvenile court that the mother had been located, and concealed the pendency of the permanent-custody decision from her, was not absolutely immune.
cases.quote: social workers are absolutely immune only when they are acting in their capacity as legal advocates - initiating court actions or testifying under oath

relevance.DEC-02: Holloway is the source of the functional test that leaves investigative and administrative caseworker conduct exposed to suit, which is what makes investigation-stage misconduct actionable at all.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the en banc decision Brent applies and quotes; a wrongful-removal claim survives only to the extent it targets conduct outside the advocacy function, and the Ohio statutory duty to seek the parents' agreement on the case plan is such conduct.

cases.case_name: Kovacic v. Cuyahoga Cty. Dept. of Children & Family Servs.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: In the first Kovacic appeal the court affirmed dismissal of the mother's Section 1983 and state tort claims as barred by Ohio's two-year limitations period, but held that the children's federal claims are not barred by Rooker-Feldman because the source of their injury is the conduct of the agency and its social workers leading up to the removal rather than the juvenile court's temporary-custody judgment.
cases.quote: the children's claims in this case do not seek review or reversal of the decision of the juvenile court to award temporary custody to the state

relevance.INP-12: This first appeal is what allowed the constitutional challenge to an Ohio emergency removal to be heard at all, and it is the predicate for the 2013 merits decision on exigency.
relevance.DEC-04: A challenge to the decision to remove is an independent federal claim, not an appeal from the juvenile court's custody order; but the parent's own claim was time-barred two years after the removal, which is the practical deadline families miss.

cases.case_name: Gersper v. Ashtabula County Children Services Board
cases.holding: Former R.C. 2151.421(G) immunized a children services board and its caseworker from a negligent-investigation suit because, although as recipients of the report they were not 'participating in the making of reports,' they did participate in the judicial proceeding that resulted from the report; the Court distinguished Brodie, where the agency received reports of abuse and failed to act at all.
cases.quote: former R.C. 2151.421(G) confers immunity upon those who, as a result of a report of a known or suspected incident of child abuse and/or neglect, participate in a judicial proceeding

relevance.INP-01: The opinion sets out who must report under R.C. 2151.421(A), the fourth-degree misdemeanor penalty for not reporting under R.C. 2151.99(A), and the agency's 24-hour duty to investigate.
relevance.INP-02: The immunity provision quoted here runs to 'anyone or any hospital, institution, school, health department, or agency participating in the making of reports,' which is the statutory protection that makes reporting by a non-mandated third party workable.
relevance.INP-06: Immunity attaches to making the report and to participating in the proceedings that follow, but not to the receiving agency's own failure to act on a report it has taken in.
relevance.INP-07: The report here came from a hospital employee, and the Court describes the health-professional reporting duty that a medical disclosure triggers.
relevance.DEC-02: An agency that investigates and goes to court on a report is immune, while Brodie denies immunity to an agency that receives reports and does nothing — the line that governs the accept-for-investigation decision.
relevance.FAIL-04: Read with Brodie, Gersper marks the boundary between immunized action on a report and the unprotected failure to act that precedes a child's serious injury.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, Seventh Appellate District, Belmont County
cases.holding: Affirming immunity for a school district and its administrators in a suit arising from a teacher's abuse of students, the court held that the R.C. 2151.421 reporting duty and the R.C. 2151.421(N) damages remedy run against the individual mandated reporters rather than against the political subdivision, and that liability attaches only where the individual had reason to suspect the abuse and failed to report.
cases.quote: Civil liability pursuant to R.C. 2151.421 only attaches when the duty to report abuse is violated.

relevance.INP-01: Skaggs applies the current version of the statute, under which the mandate runs to the individuals listed in R.C. 2151.421(B) and the damages remedy in R.C. 2151.421(N) runs against those individuals.
relevance.INP-08: It is a published application of the reporting duty to school administrators, holding that liability requires evidence that the school employee actually had reason to suspect the abuse.
relevance.FAIL-04: It shows how Ohio courts now allocate responsibility after a child is abused by a school employee, and it is a necessary check on reading Campbell as imposing liability on the district itself under the current statute.

IMMUNITY CAVEAT ON CAMPBELL v. BURTON: Yates (2004) describes the operative immunity exception as 'former R.C. 2744.02(B)(5),' so the statutory text was amended after Campbell. Campbell's 'expressly imposes liability' test nonetheless remains live and is still applied and distinguished by Ohio appellate courts — see W.H. v. Akron City School Dist. Bd. of Edn., 2025-Ohio-531 (9th Dist.), which was retrieved and read in this session for that purpose. Counsel must check the current text of R.C. 2744.02(B)(5) and R.C. 2151.421 before relying on Campbell for a failure-to-report damages claim.

MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT FOR FAMILIES (DEC-03): under Kyser v. Summit Cty. Children Servs. (2024) an Ohio children-services agency's substantiated-abuse disposition is NOT appealable under R.C. 2506.01. There is no administrative appeal to a common pleas court from a substantiation entered in SACWIS. Ohio has no reported high-court decision recognizing a due-process hearing right in a state central-registry/SACWIS listing comparable to the registry cases in other states; the federal due-process floor (Santosky; Stanley) and the confidentiality/good-cause rule of State ex rel. Clough are the nearest authority.

TROXEL IS A PLURALITY. The quoted passage is from Justice O'Connor's opinion announcing the judgment, joined by three other Justices; it is not a majority opinion. It is offered for the parental-autonomy principle, which the Ohio Supreme Court has independently stated in In re Murray.

ICWA / INP-11: no Supreme Court of Ohio decision applying ICWA was located on CourtListener. In re C.J. (10th Dist. 2018), published at 108 N.E.3d 677, is the leading published Ohio appellate ICWA decision (notice, tribal intervention, parental veto over transfer under 25 U.S.C. 1911(b), and good cause to deviate from the 25 U.S.C. 1915(b) placement preferences) and is used here, supplemented by Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl. Haaland v. Brackeen (2023) is on CourtListener only as slip-opinion and preliminary-print clusters whose retrievable text begins with the reporter's syllabus; a clean majority-text quote could not be isolated within the API budget, so it was not used. Ohio has no state ICWA statute; counsel must apply the federal act and the 2016 BIA regulations directly.

SECTION 1983 / FOURTH AMENDMENT (INP-12, DEC-02, DEC-04, FAIL-02): the Sixth Circuit controls Ohio. Kovacic arose in Cuyahoga County. Andrews (Tennessee) and Schulkers (Kentucky) arose outside Ohio but are published circuit precedent binding on Ohio federal courts. Practitioners should note the sequencing trap: Andrews established that the warrant requirement binds social workers but granted qualified immunity because the rule was not yet clearly established; Brent gives social workers absolute immunity for the contents of a removal petition, including knowingly false statements; and Bambach shows that documented parental consent will usually end both the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment claims.

NODES WITH GENUINELY THIN OHIO AUTHORITY, mapped to the nearest governing law and flagged here rather than padded: (a) DEC-06 differential/alternative response — no Ohio appellate decision on Ohio's AR track was found; mapped to the Sixth Circuit safety-plan/consent cases and Troxel. In re Perales, 52 Ohio St.2d 89, 369 N.E.2d 1047 (1977) was retrieved and read. It is the leading Ohio precedent on parental unsuitability, but no complete rule-carrying clause of 30 words or fewer could be taken from it without either dropping the 'otherwise unsuitable' alternative or including an embedded star-page marker. It is therefore represented in this brief by Hockstok v. Hockstok (2002) and In re C.R. (2006), which restate and then refine it. Note the division: Perales/Hockstok govern private parent-versus-nonparent custody disputes, while In re C.R. holds that an abuse, neglect or dependency adjudication supplies the unsuitability determination implicitly. [SUPERSEDED BY THIS PASS — Perales is now included as cluster 6865974; see the addition note below.]

Citations are taken from the CourtListener cluster records. In re A.M. (cluster 4802967) and In re Adoption of Y.E.F. (cluster 4841697) carry only the Ohio public-domain slip citation in CourtListener; their Ohio St.3d citations are not in the cluster and were not asserted. date_decided values are the CourtListener cluster date_filed; for Lassiter (cluster 110506) CourtListener records 1981-08-28, which readers should verify against the official reporter before citing a decision date.

Quotes at O'Toole (cluster 6897892) and Kyser (cluster 10680634) end at a complete clause before a trailing consequence clause ('and are immune from liability for failing to do so'; 'because the disposition does not determine a person's rights, duties, privileges, benefits, or legal relationships'). No condition or exception was dropped and no ellipses were used; the full effect of each holding is stated in the holding field.

Ohio's statutory right to counsel under R.C. 2151.352 is broader than the federal floor of Lassiter: In re Baby Girl Baxter and In re Adoption of Y.E.F. confirm that in juvenile abuse, neglect and dependency proceedings the child and the parents are entitled to counsel, appointed if indigent, at all stages. Y.E.F. extends appointed counsel on equal-protection grounds to indigent parents contesting a probate-court adoption that would terminate their rights.

Timeliness warning for FAIL-01: In re B.C. holds that due process does not entitle a parent to a delayed appeal from a permanent-custody judgment. Combined with In re Adams (continuation of temporary custody is not final and appealable), In re C.B. (denial of permanent custody plus award of legal custody to a parent is final and appealable) and now In re H.F. (the adjudication-plus-temporary-custody order must be appealed within 30 days, with no second window at disposition), these four cases determine what can be appealed and when. Missing the appeal window is ordinarily fatal in Ohio.
